item.title: Volchek: A Trailer About Meeting Circumstances with Stoicism
item.description: And that kind of stoic attitude to a circumstance that turns you into a different person really appeals to me — it may well be one of the most important skills in life, in any era.
item.content:encoded:
The very intriguing life story of Galina Volchek is coming out soon as a documentary that is titled just that, after the surname of the artistic director of the Sovremennik Theatre (a Moscow theatre) — Volchek («Волчек»).

One quote from the trailer hooked me: “The theatre ground me up.” Galina Borisovna immediately stresses that she is by no means saying this out of self-pity. And that kind of stoic attitude to a circumstance that turns you into a different person really appeals to me — it may well be one of the most important skills in life, in any era.

From 8 December you’ll be able to see on Premier (a Russian streaming service) how one of the most influential women in Russian theatre lived and worked. Before that, the film will open the Zimny film festival (an independent Russian film festival in Moscow), so that is where you can be among the first to see it.

item.title: Enchanted: Charming Humour and a Fairy Tale Without the Pomp
item.description: This series about the two daughters of the sorceress Yadviga (Elena Podkaminskaya), one of whom has to be rescued from the world of the dead, has a very charming sense of humour.
item.content:encoded:
Instead of the sixth episode of Yaga, I watched the first episode of Enchanted («Очарованные»)

There’s no Hudson Williams in blue contact lenses here, but there is the smouldering, blue-eyed, dark-haired Yuri Chursin playing Koschei (the deathless sorcerer of Russian fairy tales). Do I now want Hudson Williams to play Koschei one day? Or at least for Chursin’s Koschei to be handed one of those designer bags that Yuri’s character appraises in Severe Luxury? Yes and yes, but a girl can dream.

Anyway, back to Enchanted. This series about the two daughters of the sorceress Yadviga (Elena Podkaminskaya), one of whom has to be rescued from the world of the dead, has a very charming sense of humour. Just about everyone here gives the audience a playful wink, from the villain Verlioka (Daniil Vorobyov) to the hapless journalists of the newspaper Iskra (“The Spark”). This keeps the thick fairy-tale atmosphere from getting too pompous — and a good thing too: we’ve all had our fill of fairy tales played straight.

I liked the set-up and how squarely every actor lands their character — you believe in this universe, which means you want to keep watching.

item.title: Severe Luxury: A Knock-Off Handbag Story You Can Binge Without Guilt
item.description: This is exactly the kind of show you can put on and get hooked on without the slightest pang of guilt — because there is plenty here to get hooked on.
item.content:encoded:
Not every series released at the tail end of the year measures up to Severe Luxury («Тяжёлый люкс»). But Ilya Aksenov knows his craft: this story about dealers in knock-off designer handbags is every bit as convincing, and as daring, as Dropper.

This is exactly the kind of show you can put on and get hooked on without the slightest pang of guilt — because there is plenty here to get hooked on. Personally, I knew I was in for the long haul after the joke about a children’s entertainer who wasn’t beige enough for the birthday party of a beige mum’s child. And although at first the lens is trained squarely against Paulina Andreeva’s heroine, a rich woman with a well-off husband, the situation flips in an instant. Cruelly conned, she is rescued by her brasher brother, fresh out of prison and played by Ivan Yankovsky. As for the casting, no comment is needed: it is hard to imagine anyone better in these roles. Yuri Chursin is simply unhinged.

The first two episodes pack in a very sensible set-up, a lively partners-in-crime sequence and some fairly dark humour. It even reminded me a little of a series I love, Married Life Scenes — that one, too, is about clawing a bit of luxury out of life for yourself and your loved ones, against all the odds. So for the next month, I plan to be living in severe luxury.

And an extra point to Severe Luxury for Ivan Yankovsky in a fur coat. We have known since The Swamp that this cannot be a bad thing.

item.title: GTA VI’s Story: The Off Campus of Video Games
item.description: In short, it’s really strong dramatic writing, which now lets you feel for the characters not out of the mere thrill of the game but out of human involvement, as in a good film.
item.content:encoded:
A couple of missions into GTA VI, and I already want to revive the debate about where the line runs between a well-made video game and a feature film (especially an animated one).

And it’s no longer just about the picture. Everything has already been said about games being able to deliver visuals on a par with cinema. What interests me now is the story: it took some doing to hit so squarely today’s audience demand for non-toxic (as far as that’s possible) male characters and female partners who are their equals.

Laugh if you like, but to my mind GTA VI could be called the Off Campus of the video game world. Well, why not: a backstory in which the relationship starts out from dislike — check; a reason why they can’t be together — check; a caring relationship (even in a criminal setting) — that’s there too. In short, it’s really strong dramatic writing, which now lets you feel for the characters not out of the mere thrill of the game but out of human involvement, as in a good film.

I had bet that this game would be interesting to watch precisely as a viewer, and I was absolutely right.

item.title: Rare: An Unconventional Way to Talk About Children with Rare Diseases
item.description: In the film, excerpts from rehearsals alternate with scenes at home in which we get to know the families who took part in the filming, so the atmosphere is as warm and sincere as can be, and the pace never lets you get bored.
item.content:encoded:
A very unusual documentary, Rare, came out today — a unique attempt to talk about children (and people in general, for that matter) with rare genetic diseases in an unconventional format. Personally, I’m always very glad when projects like this appear — I think they hold the kind of soft power that roots out intolerance and fear of the unknown.

The film is built from behind-the-scenes footage of the preparations for the play Moy obychny | redky den («Мой обычный | редкий день», “My Ordinary | Rare Day”), which was put together from children’s reflections on the idea of rarity. I should make clear here that the production, directed by Ksenia Sadovski, really did take place: it was staged at the Pushkin Theatre (a Moscow theatre), and the actors Darya Ekamasova and Artur Beschastny appeared on stage. It was a creative process in the truest sense, a shared search for answers to far-from-trivial questions. In the film, excerpts from rehearsals alternate with scenes at home in which we get to know the families who took part in the filming, so the atmosphere is as warm and sincere as can be, and the pace never lets you get bored. And — a great rarity — the poster conveys the mood on screen 1000%: if that kind of promise of hope on the horizon speaks to you, it is definitely worth watching.

I’m glad to be telling you about this film, because I want people, when rare diseases are mentioned, not to take fright or feel awkward but to understand that behind the diagnosis there is a whole person and a rare love of life, in spite of all the difficulties. But the director, Roman Travaye, put it best:

“This film was made to help those who feel lonely or lost in the face of a diagnosis, and for those who take a broader view of the world”

It is worth remembering that there are far more such people right around us than it might seem. You can already watch Rare on VK Video (a Russian video platform).

item.title: Minotaur: A Final Shot That Fills In Every Gap
item.description: An enormous effect achieved with the simplest of means — real cinema, like the whole of Minotaur.
item.content:encoded:
One of the things that stayed with me most after Minotaur is its final shot. I won’t spoil what is in it, but let me put this on record: if you get the chance to see the film, give that shot your full, undivided attention.

After following the characters down a contentious, much-debated path, we arrive at the last shot. It is a very simple one. I will say only that its effect on me was comparable to the revelation that hits Jim Carrey’s character in The Truman Show when, in the film’s final scene, his boat reaches the horizon. A complete, irreversible understanding of how everything works, how it has been and how it always will be, for as long as humanity exists. Of the price paid by the characters who make it to the end, and the price paid by us, the viewers, who have been breathing the air of that very same time.

I can’t help admiring it: the film had any number of chances to fall into the trap of “nudging” the viewer towards one reading of events or another, and instead it sets that viewer adrift in the back alleys of their own unconscious, with all the trauma and scars life has left them. No blunt moral, no lecturing from the author, no sermonising verdicts on the fate of an era — only complete freedom to understand, as far as your own existential crisis allows.

Russian punctuation has a term, ottochie («отточие»): a row of dots that fills a gap in a text. Well, this shot is the perfect ottochie: look closely enough and it fills every gap, question and assumption in the film you have just watched. An enormous effect achieved with the simplest of means — real cinema, like the whole of Minotaur.

item.title: Ayda!: Inevitably Compared with The Boy’s Word, Best Judged on Its Own Terms
item.description: All in all, the story certainly deserves attention; it just ought to be judged by laws other than those instilled in us by the series that introduced the word ‘chushpan’.
item.content:encoded:
Ayda! («Айда») will not escape comparisons with The Boy’s Word (Slovo patsana, the 2023 Russian hit series), and I won’t try to escape them either.

The series follows Grisha (Aleksey Onezhen), who falls in with the Tyap-Lyap gang after moving to Kazan in 1978, and it opens with none of the boyish charm that, as I remember it, made the first scenes of Palto and little Marat’s friendship so captivating. There is a structural reason for that, too: in The Boy’s Word the boys joined ‘the street’ of their own accord, from below, whereas in Ayda! the path is laid out for them by a seductive adult mentor, played by Daniil Vorobyov. Hence no romance whatsoever — only good old ultraviolence.

It is a pleasure to watch Aleksey Onezhen take on a deeply dramatic character: until now I had mostly seen him in comic roles (thanks to the sweet series Pride, «Гордость»), and here he shows new sides. The rest of the cast draw the eye as well, but I am especially curious about the leader of the Komsomol combat squad (a Soviet youth vigilante patrol), played by Anton Artemyev: he is the opposite pole to ‘the street’, the one lucky enough to have been handed a licence for violence. All in all, the story certainly deserves attention; it just ought to be judged by laws other than those instilled in us by the series that introduced the word ‘chushpan’ (its term for a kid outside the gangs).

item.title: My Friend AI: The Series Where Svyatoslav Rogozhan Lucked Out with His Role
item.description: This story of artificial intelligence in the service of a good guy is a very brisk and good-naturedly naive watch, which is sometimes just the thing.
item.content:encoded:
There are shows where particular actors really luck out with a role.

In the series My Friend AI («Мой друг — ИИ»), for instance, the lucky one is Svyatoslav Rogozhan. He plays the human embodiment of an AI assistant, and the result is not merely the opposite of a shy eleventh-grader but a full-blown trickster, a Tyler Durden, an evil genius and anyone else you care to name with villainous charisma. Watching him in this kind of part is a real pleasure.

The modest high-schooler played by Kai Getts, on the other hand, is supposed to arouse pity and, judging by the plot, to look like an ugly duckling, but that is impossible to believe. And although the characters work very well as a duo, he and his spirited AI friend, this mismatch of types is hard to ignore.

In any case, this story of artificial intelligence in the service of a good guy is a very brisk and good-naturedly naive watch, which is sometimes just the thing :)

item.title: Heads of State: Naishuller’s Latest Is a Decent, Fun Action Film with Its Caveats
item.description: Naishuller’s latest isn’t bad: Heads of State, with John Cena and Idris Elba. It’s a fun action film, though it comes with its caveats.
item.content:encoded:
Naishuller’s latest isn’t bad: Heads of State, with John Cena and Idris Elba. It’s a fun action film, though it comes with its caveats. I’ve sorted it into pluses and minuses:

➕ A wonderful killer cyborg played by Aleksandr Kuznetsov. He goes at the part with downright ferocious commitment, no joke. I was rooting for him to the very end, purely for his villainous charisma.

➕ A side-splittingly funny scene with Belarusian gopniks (street thugs). Heaps of swearing that sounds like home, the peculiarities of doing battle in the countryside, and the unforgettable line “gopnik leader” in the credits. The punks and the leading politicians alike are sent packing by a simple farm woman played by Ingeborga Dapkunaite, and between the blows there’s an elegant nod to the “general’s ticker” meme (kotly, Russian slang for a wristwatch).

➕ A worthy cameo from the director. Ilya Naishuller yells “kurwa” with total abandon in the guise of a Polish policeman.

➕ A mess of global proportions is sorted out, by and large, by one delicate young woman. The kowtow to female power is duly noted.

➖ There’s just one minus, but it’s a matter of logic, and so a big fat one. The catalyst for the action, the characters’ motivation and any rationale whatsoever for what’s going on are so sketchy and flat (“if there’s political instability in the US and England, NATO will scatter in a second”) that the effect is comic, this time in a bad way. Some sort of storm in a teacup full of subjunctives.

item.title: The Most Niche Selection of Films to Watch on Holiday
item.description: A short list of what I watched and rewatched on my beach holiday: The Impossible, The Godfather, The Devil’s Advocate and Our Oceans.
item.content:encoded:
The most niche selection of films to watch on holiday.

For your attention, a short list of what I watched and rewatched on my beach holiday:

  • The Impossible, a 2012 disaster film about the miraculous rescue of one family during the 2004 tsunami. The worst possible film to watch on holiday by the ocean: it instantly reminds you that the idyll of palm trees and brightly coloured fish is, in fact, the wild, which can at any moment, as cold-bloodedly as you like, spring a surprise in the form of a mass disaster. As a piece of filmmaking it’s tremendously powerful: everything to do with the characters’ ordeals is conveyed so convincingly that you feel it physically. A bonus is Tom Holland’s wonderful debut performance, which, incidentally, won him several awards.

  • The Godfather (Parts I and II): a rewatch in both cases. A classic that needs no comment.

  • The Devil’s Advocate: a first viewing and, of course, not without a wish to see Al Pacino in a different context after the Godfathers. The ending threw me: it’s a superb reversal that can surprise you again and again. Along the way I caught some frightening resemblances* between Keanu Reeves and a certain young actor of today, but when has that ever been a problem. The protagonist’s creepy smile at the start of the film goes into the collection alongside Oleg Menshikov’s unforgettable bared-teeth grin in Burnt by the Sun.

  • Our Oceans, a Netflix documentary series about the oceans and their inhabitants. It was chosen to restore the balance of my nervous system after The Impossible, and it more than did the job. It’s not often you get to see so much that’s new about the oceans and the outlandish creatures that live in them. The fish are beautiful, the footage is as high-quality and detailed as it gets, and the narrator’s voice, supplied by Barack Obama, is perfectly convincing.

item.title: Minotaur: When Poisoned Air Becomes the Protagonist
item.description: If the phrase “poisoned air” ever needs to be visualised, you can safely point to Minotaur as the perfect example.
item.content:encoded:
If the phrase “poisoned air” ever needs to be visualised, you can safely point to Minotaur as the perfect example.

In September 2022 Gleb (Dmitriy Mazurov), a provincial businessman, finds himself saddled not only with family trouble (his wife Galina is cheating on him) but also with a demand from above: to pick 14 of his employees for mobilisation. Making decisions that nobody would ever want to make (though on that point there is a wonderful scene comparing how Gleb and his businessman friends see the situation), the hero barely notices how his own self is changing. Taking this not exactly pleasant but very believable walk with Gleb through the back alleys of a readiness to compromise is gripping at the very least; at most, it leaves you dumbstruck.

As soon as the first news of Minotaur appeared, I shamelessly read the whole plot on Wikipedia, because I knew that what mattered here was not what exactly would happen, but how. I turned out to be right. This is not just a big festival film; it is practically an imprint of a particular moment in our shared life, the everyday signs of a universal, irreversible transformation sealed inside the frame. And of course, to convey the nature of what I saw, I want to reach for associations with the classics 👇

First, the film has a scene whose cruelty is comparable, perhaps, only to Korean cinema. The closest fit here is Bong Joon-ho’s Parasite, where for most of the running time the viewer is weighed down by the bleakest social irony, and then at the climax things turn truly brutal on the physical level too. For two hours we watch how the characters came to this, and for three minutes we actually see what exactly they have come to.

Second, the urban environment that ends up on screen matters a great deal. As it happens, my degree thesis was on precisely this subject, “The Representation of the Urban Environment in European Cinema: The Case of Auteur Film of the 1950s–1960s” — it’s even funny that back then it hardly crossed my mind to look to contemporary cinema for urban subtexts, whereas now I would of course give Minotaur a place of its own in that study. For the films of the New Wave it was fundamentally important to achieve documentary realism on screen, which is why the action was taken out into the streets. Its attention to the details of urban space gives Minotaur exactly that: a realism that plunges you into a kind of paralysing déjà vu, right down to the typeface on the posters or the shades of the passers-by’s clothes. It’s worth mentioning that in the films of the European New Wave (let’s count Italian neorealism and the Soviet Thaw in here too), buildings destroyed in the Second World War kept flashing past on screen as the backdrop to many characters’ state of mind. What flashes past behind the irreversible inner rearrangement of Minotaur’s characters we have seen with our own eyes, so on screen it hits twice as hard.

I’d like to watch Minotaur once more with the option of pausing, skipping back and forth and studying the shots: there is more than enough detail to pore over, from the actors’ subtle facial expressions and the moments when Evgueni Galperine’s singular music rises and dies away, to the tiniest lettering in the background. I hope the chance will come up in the near future.

item.title: Mirror at the Vnutri Theatre: A Cabaret with Notes of Armageddon
item.description: The plot is based half on Heinrich Böll’s story “Murke’s Collected Silences” and half on Kurt Vonnegut’s novel Slaughterhouse-Five. It left a colossal impression.
item.content:encoded:
On to theatrical discoveries

Recently I was lucky enough to catch a show with Savva Savelyev and Pavel Tabakov called Mirror. It is staged by the theatre space Vnutri, which describes its genre as a detective cabaret, but there I would disagree. It is more of a cabaret with notes of armageddon: when the worst has already happened and all that is left is to say “never mind, on with the waltz”.

The plot is based half on Heinrich Böll’s story “Murke’s Collected Silences” and half on Kurt Vonnegut’s novel Slaughterhouse-Five, and, as you can easily guess, it deals with a specific historical event. Here the devastating bombing of Dresden is worked through by way of a chance collision between witnesses to it from different generations: they share a traumatic background but hold completely different truths.

Savva Savelyev and Pavel Tabakov play this story as a two-hander, but they have energy to spare for the several decades of context the production draws on. A simple situation escalates into an ideological clash of catastrophic proportions, and that doesn’t let you switch off from what is happening for a second. Although the temptation to look away is, as in life, very great.

It left a colossal impression, so I do recommend the show.

item.title: Wicker: The Fairy Tale We Deserve
item.description: Wicker is, quite literally, the fairy tale we deserve. This parable about how it is best to live by your own lights speaks a very economical yet expressive language.
item.content:encoded:
Wicker (released in Russia as Pletyony muzh, “The Wicker Husband”) is, quite literally, the fairy tale we deserve.

This parable about how it is best to live by your own lights speaks a very economical yet expressive language — in its script, its visuals and its symbolism alike. The medieval world of the little town where the story unfolds is built so painstakingly and inventively that you seem to tumble right into it and find yourself standing in the middle of the street.

On top of that, the characters have no names, only their trades: the Basketmaker (Peter Dinklage), the Fisherwoman (Olivia Colman), the Bottlewasher and others. The forms of address say a good deal about how this society is arranged, too: every woman except the heroine serves as an appendage to her husband — the Tailor’s Wife (or the Doctor’s Daughter), the Baker’s Wife, the Innkeeper’s Wife. Their own husbands don’t have much respect for them either, which is hardly surprising.

But what they enjoy most of all is ganging up on the Fisherwoman: she has no husband, you see, so she is less than whole. Colman’s heroine is hounded so badly that she goes to the Basketmaker and asks him to weave her a husband (he is played by Alexander Skarsgård), and that is where the most interesting part begins. Life in the town gets no better at all now that every member of society is living in a traditional marriage, but the Fisherwoman’s life changes forever. How other people’s happiness infuriates people, and how hard it is to defend yourself against that hatred — that is what the whole rest of the film is devoted to: one of the wisest films, and at the same time one of the most modest in its means of expression.

You can see this love and lovelessness in Russian cinemas from 5 November, courtesy of @provzglyad.

item.title: Yaga: A Supernatural Mystery for a Gloomy Autumn
item.description: This is a very solid, very tight supernatural mystery. For a gloomy autumn it’s downright ideal.
item.content:encoded:
The first episodes of the series Yaga are finally out.

This is a very solid, very tight supernatural mystery. For a gloomy autumn it’s downright ideal. Private detective Rapp arrives in a backwater town to look for Henry Park, the missing son of rich parents, and plunges headlong into petty local intrigues. Only nobody is exactly rushing to help him — not Carson, the local policewoman, not Professor Katherine, not the missing Henry’s roommate (who for some reason is the spitting image of him — both characters are played by Hudson Williams). And then all manner of supernatural goings-on make themselves felt: not a moment’s peace for the characters or for the audience.

They make 100% use of the play’s text, which I had got to grips with in advance. But even better is the part of the action built on top of it, devised by the show’s writers. The two episodes go by in a single breath, and I hope the rest are made in the same spirit. The IC3PEAK song (the band has been designated a “foreign agent” in Russia) fits the neon party scene perfectly. Evidently, Russian songs at raves are now a must-have for series on the streaming service Crave.

item.title: The Seventh Player: Ted Lasso, Hockey-Style
item.description: Judging by the first episode, the main impression so far is one of commotion. This time Anton Lapenko has, if anything, been handed “himself in the given circumstances” to play.
item.content:encoded:
I’ve started watching The Seventh Player — art imitates life, Ted Lasso the KHL (Russia’s Kontinental Hockey League), as they say.

Judging by the first episode, the main impression so far is one of commotion, but one thing is clear: this time Anton Lapenko has been handed “himself in the given circumstances” to play rather than one of the stock types (those, mind you, are covered by the other characters). That’s rather interesting, because within the plot, too, his character is forever the odd one out, being “outside the system” (whether in relation to his wealthy family or to his own hockey team). So there’s at least one reason to follow the action.

But — I very much want to believe there will be slightly fewer music-video-style scenes from here on, because they water the pace down a great deal, and atmosphere can be created by other means too. For example, by the rather well-shot inserts of hockey matches.

item.title: Kat Sandler’s Play Yaga: Baba Yaga Without the Stereotypes
item.description: In Kat Sandler’s play, the Baba Yaga we know is no exotic souvenir on the shelf of Canadian drama but a fully fledged, modern heroine.
item.content:encoded:
While waiting for the series Yaga with Hudson Williams, I read the play it’s based on and came away filled to the brim

I adore it when Russian culture is woven into Western works without the crude stereotypes (what we call “cranberry”), and even more so when such things get a screen adaptation.

In Kat Sandler’s play, the Baba Yaga we know is no exotic souvenir on the shelf of Canadian drama but a fully fledged, modern heroine who thinks about her own attractiveness, craves the company of handsome men and radiates the kind of woman power you rarely come across. The text has absorbed the morphology of the folktale and the standards of contemporary playwriting as if the two traditions had been made for each other.

For anyone planning to watch the supernatural true-crime series from 23 October, it’s almost required reading. And to everyone who is simply interested in contemporary literature, I simply recommend it very highly — in many ways it’s a unique experience :)

item.title: Half-Life: An Image of Impersonal Danger from the First Episode
item.description: Having events unfold in two eras in parallel really suits a story about nuclear tests in the USSR.
item.content:encoded:
16 October 2026

I can’t think what posters could capture the mood of Half-Life, right from its first episode, better than these. A confrontation with an impersonal source of danger that is all but impossible to fight is an image that is quite in demand.

Having events unfold in two eras in parallel really suits a story about nuclear tests in the USSR. And it’s good that we enter this story through Anna Mikhalkova’s character: you want to believe her and to watch this heroine find out the truth.

15 November 2026

Half-Life leaves an indelible impression if you watch three or four episodes in a row. I grew attached to the characters and waited with dread for the episode with the explosion itself. It turned out not to be the most frightening sight in the series.

The moment of the actual tests is, of course, horrifying. And the cutaways to the observation bunker with Zhukov and Kurchatov (the marshal and the head of the Soviet atomic project) drive out the very last scraps of faith in humanity. But right alongside are the fates of the female student volunteers, the conscripts and the villagers (even beyond the main characters’ family), who almost always remain human. That is exactly why the most frightening part of the series turns out to be the ominous “after” that comes for each of them. I hope that in the two remaining episodes the epithet that fits the fate of the characters who survived the explosion will give way to a more life-affirming one.

On a separate note, I still can’t figure out the nature of the photographer Veniamin Krasnov (Dmitry Chebotarev). He seems to be equal parts human warmth and the fanaticism of a man steeped in war through and through. Where a cocktail like that leads, perhaps we’ll yet see.

P.S. The chemistry between Mikhalkova’s and Yankovsky’s characters is something incredible. For me it tops the list of the most unexpected casting successes among actors who have to play deep, warm feelings.

27 November 2026

You could talk about Half-Life for a long time, but the main thing to remember is that the finale of a story this tense is under no obligation whatsoever to be spectacular in the cinematic sense.

We saw the explosion itself and its aftermath, but the final battle was fought entirely in offices, behind closed doors, in the interiors of ministries. It’s both unusual and, in its own way, mesmerising: literally “Nadezhda against all” (Nadezhda, Anna Mikhalkova’s heroine, whose name means “hope”). In both the literal and the figurative sense.

I’ll be waiting very impatiently for the next projects with Ioann Kochkin (he played the soldier Yura) — my main acting discovery from Half-Life, simply bravo! He played love, clowning, longing, cunning, despair — you couldn’t list it all. And all the other actors seemed to open up to me afresh as well, from Filipp Yankovsky to Petar Zekavica.

P.S. I liked the way the term “half-life” sounded in Maxim Stoyanov’s final line. His best line of the season.

item.title: The Forest: A Meditative Canvas for Bad Weather
item.description: In Russian cinemas from 15 October, The Forest (Les. Khranitel zhizni) is a feature-length meditative canvas with the most breathtaking views of forests and the creatures that live in them.
item.content:encoded:
While nature is treating us to less than lovely weather, you can enjoy picturesque landscapes in a cinema.

In Russian cinemas from 15 October, The Forest (Les. Khranitel zhizni, “The Forest. Keeper of Life”) is a feature-length meditative canvas with the most breathtaking views of forests and the creatures that live in them. There’s birdwatching, there’s a touch of V mire zhivotnykh (“In the Animal World”, the classic Soviet and Russian nature programme), and there’s macro footage of things the eye couldn’t make out even if you were standing in the forest yourself.

The crew went on 14 expeditions to capture the primeval forest. The sounds were recorded separately, and they are another of the film’s surprises. All in all, the most soothing documentary in a long while :)

item.title: You’ve Got Mail: Autumn Cosiness with Tom Hanks and Meg Ryan
item.description: If you’re more and more often in the mood for something autumnally cosy, let me remind you of the film You’ve Got Mail, with Tom Hanks and Meg Ryan.
item.content:encoded:
If you’re more and more often in the mood for something autumnally cosy, let me remind you of the film You’ve Got Mail, with Tom Hanks and Meg Ryan.

This story of two bookshop owners who are rivals in real life but turn out to be anonymous pen pals online is told in a wonderful, life-affirming style. As a bonus, you get the aesthetic of analogue devices, now enjoying a modest renaissance among the young, a terrific script and even dashes of the “screenlife from 1998” genre. And given how smoothly the film’s mood drifts from autumn into Christmas and New Year, it is especially timely for the months ahead.

Watching it has some interesting side effects as well: set it beside Russian films from the late 1990s and about the 1990s, and you may get the sense of a parallel reality. The characters in You’ve Got Mail have lactose-free decaf from Starbucks, gyms and online correspondence, while the characters in a Russian film from roughly the same period have New Russians (the flashy new rich of the 1990s), property scams and everyday disarray amid a capitalism that descended on them out of nowhere.

item.title: Leviticus: A Modest Horror Made with Taste
item.description: I watched Leviticus (the Russian title is a straight translation, Levit), and it’s made modestly but with taste: like a good old no-nonsense horror flick.
item.content:encoded:
On the subject of horror films.

I watched Leviticus (the Russian title is a straight translation, Levit), and it’s made modestly but with taste: like a good old no-nonsense horror flick, built on a fairly tight budget. In the story, a religious community tries to fight teenage infatuation with terror-inducing rites — and, contrary to the ritual’s purpose, an evil spirit takes possession of everyone who has been through the “cleansing”. The nastiest part: it appears in the guise of the person they love and tries to kill them every time.

What looks especially fresh next to the slow-burn horrors now in fashion is the half-ordinary, man-in-the-street view of what is going on: some small-town school, some little circle of sermon-goers, the stuff of everyday life; the existential horror behind it all still has to be made out, and it isn’t thrust at you from the first frame.

The running time is very modest, but you don’t need any more, because you feel for the characters on a human level: I mean, what kind of cruel joke is it when you can’t tell whether the person in front of you is real or their disembodied killer double. I’m glad I watched it, and I like the idea that in our world your own feelings are the last thing you should be afraid of.

item.title: Race to Monte Carlo: The Escapism of Silver Skates, the Adrenaline of F1
item.description: Race to Monte Carlo recaptures the singular escapist mood of Silver Skates and at the same time outdoes F1 for sheer drive in its racing scenes. And all this with an almost fairy-tale story, which here actually works in its favour.
item.content:encoded:
Race to Monte Carlo (Bitva motorov, “Battle of Motors”) recaptures the singular escapist mood of Silver Skates and at the same time (to my mind) outdoes F1 for sheer drive in its racing scenes. And all this with an almost fairy-tale story (which here actually works in its favour).

The film, about the development and fleeting triumph of the first car built in the Russian Empire, has absorbed the best of both the Russian and the Hollywood traditions. It manages to cross the American dream with a road movie and an unashamedly sentimental view of a pre-revolutionary aesthetic that has long since vanished. At the height of its idealising, the film even lets you forget such basics as class divisions; in this it follows the example of Silver Skates. Impossible, but so good. Technically, Race to Monte Carlo is on very solid ground too: the racing scenes are stunning, with a nerve you can almost touch, and the costumes, sets and period cars catch the eye as well. The supporting ensemble is superbly written and played.

What pulls you in, of course, is the dynamic between Ivan Yankovsky’s and Yura Borisov’s characters: they are the film’s real engines. The wily, virtuosically brazen motoring enthusiast Andrey Nagel is the lead for the first part of the film, and he balances, fair and square, somewhere between the uncompromising Bokov from Fisher and the many-faced Adidas from The Boy’s Word. Dmitry Bondarev, in whom an engineer’s passion gradually awakens, is if anything slightly more interesting to watch: there are contradictions in him, a distrust of the world and an unbreakable spirit. The duo is written really well and vividly, even if it does not quite square with the historical facts about Russo-Balt.

There is one weak spot: the central heroine, a car enthusiast played by Paulina Andreeva, is slotted far too schematically into the inventors’ competitive friendship. She appears and disappears like a strictly scripted plot device and, sadly, never becomes a full-blooded character (unlike, say, the heroine of Silver Skates). Another curiosity (whether it works or not is for each viewer to decide) is Emperor Nicholas II: pointedly adorable, there is no other word for it, he both backs the car inventors and brushes aside the chief antagonist’s denunciations. Unlike the wicked officials who very nearly wrecked Nagel’s entire car business.

All in all, it is worth seeing: this is big cinema, and it can rightly be called both a thrill ride and a sentimental reconstruction of a world lost for ever; however you take it, it will impress you.

Off to think about the Roman Russian Empire.

item.title: The KHL as a Series: The “Mic on the Referee” Segment
item.description: What has really won me over is the “Mic on the Referee/Player” segment. Now that is true mockumentary, with a comic slant and an unpredictable plot.
item.content:encoded:
I keep half an eye on the KHL (Russia’s Kontinental Hockey League; now and then I even cheer for Torpedo, on the same inexplicable principle that has me cheering for Croatia in football).

But what has really won me over is the “Mic on the Referee/Player” segment. That’s when every remark and wisecrack let loose on the ice becomes public property (except that the bleeping gets in the way) :)

Now that is true mockumentary, with a comic slant and an unpredictable plot. What’s more, such interesting behind-the-scenes details sometimes surface that you feel like praising the creators for their meticulous world-building. Now I know, for instance, that at the Volga Arena in Nizhny Novgorod the little door onto the ice is rigged so cunningly that not a single member of the officiating crew could get the better of it.

item.title: Facts to Take In: Hipsters and 9th Company Have an Identical Ending
item.description: From the “facts to take in” column: Hipsters and 9th Company have exactly the same ending. Plus a few more unexpected parallels (with spoilers).
item.content:encoded:
From the “facts to take in” column: Hipsters (Stilyagi, 2008) and 9th Company (9 rota, 2005) have exactly the same ending. Plus a few more unexpected parallels (with spoilers):

  • The two films’ endings are built to an absolutely identical blueprint. All film long the heroes have been making a sacrifice (the hipsters expressing themselves at the cost of their place in society, the soldiers in Afghanistan “defending the motherland” and literally dying), and in the end it turns out that nobody needed that sacrifice in the slightest and it was made for nothing (there are, it emerges, no hipsters in America, and so no freedom in being one either, while the top brass simply forgot about the 9th Company). But in their hearts the protagonists of both films are absolutely certain they have won — the final shots say so outright: both the closing speech by Lyuty, the sole survivor, and the jubilant dance of Shagin’s and Akinshina’s characters in a crowd of other nonconformists from every era of Russian subculture that followed.

  • The films share a screenwriter, Yuri Korotkov. That partly explains both the first point and the next couple. But you have to admit it’s remarkable how one and the same script blueprint works for a war drama and for a period dramedy musical.

  • Neither film has a clear-cut villain — the role goes to an impersonal system which, come to think of it, could go by the same name in both cases: “the state apparatus”. The indifferent machine catches up with hipsters and conscripts alike; there is essentially no one to hate, only heroes, each a sharply drawn type, to feel sorry for — very convenient.

  • The heroes’ identities are interesting too. Soldiers and hipsters alike have nicknames in place of names. Were our characters to swap places, the nicknames Vorobey (“Sparrow”) and Gioconda would fit right in with the fashionable crowd, and Bob and Dryn (“Cudgel”) in the barracks. The viewer is faced with characters who are easy to connect with, while the villain in both films is faced with a faceless mass that isn’t even worth addressing by name.

  • The figure of a woman whom the film’s heroes accept but whom society, outside the extreme situation the characters live in, would condemn. Snow White in 9th Company and Polza in Hipsters break patriarchal taboos and serve as symbols rather than fully rounded people. Even so, they make a perfect backdrop for the saintliness of the protagonists, whom, once again, we pity because the system is crushing them.

Food for thought.

item.title: Nimrods: The Film Green Day Produced
item.description: The road movie about teenage punks who dream of making it onto the big stage is called Nimrods. In short, a great genre film with bits of concert sprinkled in.
item.content:encoded:
As tradition demands, at the end of September I remembered the band Green Day (thanks, naturally, to the line “wake me up when September ends”). And it turns out they have produced a pretty decent film.

The road movie about teenage punks who dream of making it onto the big stage is called Nimrods (English slang for “dimwits”). Tommy, Fred and Chad are mad about Green Day and set off across America fully convinced that the band have invited them to open their big New Year’s concert. And although nothing goes to plan, the boys grow up, discover the world and, as befits a film whose finale is steeped in New Year atmosphere, pick up some timeless values. There are clichés and contrivances in the plot, of course, but they come across more as part of the humour and don’t spoil things at all.

In short, a great genre film with bits of concert sprinkled in (you can top up your playlist afterwards). All the actors are completely at home in their roles, the teenagers and the older generation alike. By a funny coincidence, the bit parts include Jenna Fischer and Angela Kinsey, the famous Pam and Angela from The Office. It’s great when all the elements of an idea come together to winning effect, and that is exactly the case here.

item.title: Girlyanda: A Graphic Novel About an Artist with a Claw
item.description: I bought Girlyanda (“Garland”) blind, won over by the blurb about its hero, a comics artist whose hand has turned into a claw.
item.content:encoded:
Impressed by a graphic novel once again

I bought Girlyanda («Гирлянда», “Garland”) blind, won over by the blurb about its hero, a comics artist whose hand has turned into a claw. Admit it, we’ve all been there: you’re going about your life, bothering no one, and suddenly some important part of you changes for good.

I read it with great pleasure in two sittings: the plot hooks you, and the atmosphere of a snowy city in the run-up to New Year is thrown in as a gift. Best of all, the comic itself is like a box with a false bottom: because the protagonist runs comics-drawing workshops in the story, we as readers pick up some of the nuts and bolts too, and even get a few reading recommendations.

So I’m recommending Girlyanda in my turn — if only so you can join the protagonist in working through his dilemma.

item.title: Five Russian Shorts from the Days of Russian-Cypriot Cinema
item.description: I watched almost the entire shorts programme at the Days of Russian-Cypriot Cinema festival, and there are 5 of the Russian films I want to share.
item.content:encoded:
Yesterday I watched almost the entire shorts programme at the Days of Russian-Cypriot Cinema festival, and there are 5 of the Russian films I want to share with you. If you get the chance, watch them too: they are wonderful.

  • Mama prosila ne vzryvat meteorit (“Mum Asked Me Not to Blow Up the Meteorite”) is a charming story about a boy from a snowbound village who befriends a meteorite and decides to help it gather up all the pieces that have broken off it. Enchanting magical realism (a cool trick that is by now the trademark of the studio Red Pepper Film) and a lead actor who holds 100% of your attention, Yaroslav Golovnev.

  • Cold Shower is a compact story about second chances, for yourself and for others. The forty-year-old heroine is a single mother who works at the sorting centre of an unnamed online marketplace and so, naturally, is not rolling in money. At work she has a subordinate: a kidult through and through, forever late but impossibly sweet, with a charming smile, a flask of fragrant coffee and his signature sandwiches at the ready. How could you not fall in love, especially when it’s mutual? But the guy comes trailing problems of his own, and they will have to sort them out together.

  • Kak my deda provozhali (“How We Saw Grandad Off”) is another Red Pepper Film production, and one that, incidentally, won the festival’s top prize. A family that has fallen out travels to bury the grandfather; since his passing, relations between the generations have gone completely sour. Only a miracle can reconcile the two sides, but it won’t be quite the usual kind. My sincere admiration for the light pouring out of the screen and for the most mouth-watering vatrushki (sweet cheese buns) in contemporary Russian cinema.

  • Marusya: the USSR, shortages, ration cards. Marusya, a thief (an incredible performance by Alexandra Bolshakova), is trying to carry an expensive chandelier out of a flat so she can make a run for the Black Sea. It turns out that the flat is home to a naive mother with a baby, holy simplicity itself, who doesn’t even realise that the father has abandoned them. Marusya faces a hard moral choice, and watching it play out is a real psychological drama.

  • Vremya kormit golubey (“Time to Feed the Pigeons”) is another short about the wise, the good and the eternal, in which the only thing that gave me pause was how carefree the hero is in the face of expulsion from university, unrealistic by the standards of 2026. To cheer up his grandmother, her student grandson recreates a pigeon-feeding scene beneath her windows and, it seems, gets what he was after

item.title: Smaragda: An Unhurried Film That Exceeded Expectations
item.description: Smaragda turned out to be an unhurried film, but therein lies its wisdom. If films about the philosophy of life are your thing, this one is for you.
item.content:encoded:
Smaragda turned out to be an unhurried film, but therein lies its wisdom. Taken all together, it exceeded my expectations.

After her mother’s death the heroine suddenly discovers that she has been left on the sidelines: they want to make a young colleague with a blog and followers the presenter of the programme that Smaragda devised from start to finish, and her health keeps throwing up problems. Her personal life, too, is a long way from stable and happy. At an existential dead end, Smaragda starts a blog about environmental problems and, along the way, gets to know herself all over again.

You could compare the film to Fleabag or The Worst Person in the World, and that would be fair. But the Cypriot version stands out for its gentler tone and its attention to the heroine’s inner world. If films about the philosophy of life are your thing, this one is for you.

item.title: Gorbushka. The Heart of Russian Rock: A Video Memoir, a Concert and a Hint of the Mystical
item.description: After watching the documentary-concert Gorbushka. The Heart of Russian Rock, I caught myself thinking that there is something utterly Solovyov-like about the directing here.
item.content:encoded:
After watching the documentary-concert Gorbushka. The Heart of Russian Rock, I caught myself thinking that there is something utterly Solovyov-like about the directing here.

Of course, the connection with the methods of Sergei Solovyov (the director of Assa) lies not in direct echoes but purely in the atmosphere: when, within a single work, the hot somehow starts to go together with the blue and the prickly — that’s it. A documentary series about the rockers whose prime was spent at the Gorbunov House of Culture (the Moscow venue known as Gorbushka), it is a video memoir, a concert and even a hint of the mystical, with a parallel storyline. And as a bonus, it’s a wonderful chance to top up your playlist.

If you love documentaries and true, home-grown Russian rock, I recommend it unreservedly.

item.title: Mayday: I Nearly Switched It Off 15 Minutes In, and That Would Have Been a Mistake
item.description: Mayday starts out as a dull, pompous Hollywood action B-movie, but that’s a test of your staying power.
item.content:encoded:
I nearly switched this film off 15 minutes in (hence the meme, as it happens).

Mayday starts out as a dull, pompous Hollywood action B-movie, but that’s a test of your staying power. Everyone who manages to push through that stage will be rewarded with a wonderful comedy (at one moment, at the very least, I was laughing out loud).

It’s 1987, and Troy (Reynolds), a downed American reconnaissance pilot, ends up the prisoner guest of Nikolai (Kenneth Branagh’s character insists on being called Nick). The Soviet citizen turns out to be a fervent fan of America: his home is decked out in the appropriate merch, and his favourite film is Top Gun with Tom Cruise 🇺🇸 While helping Troy get home, Nick himself gets fired up by the dream of asylum in the US, so he bravely (and just as ludicrously) goes through every stage of the escape from the USSR alongside his new-found friend.

Despite a certain amount of inevitable “cranberry” (crude Russian clichés) and naivety, Mayday is good as a reminder that having a laugh at yourself is sometimes very healthy. And if you enjoy hearing people in films speak English with a thick Russian accent, watch it undubbed.

item.title: Matty Manson’s Razlomy: Prose That Pulled a Fast One on Me
item.description: So I started reading Matty Manson’s novel Razlomy (“Fractures”) — a sweet urban fantasy about a guy called Vinny who can relay the most intimate questions to the universe.
item.content:encoded:
Contemporary Russian prose that pulled a fast one on me

So I started reading Matty Manson’s novel Razlomy («Разломы», “Fractures”) — a sweet urban fantasy about a guy called Vinny who can relay the most intimate questions to the universe, while he himself has been tormented since the age of 13 by the mystery of his mum’s disappearance. Oh, and he’s a bit of a punk, so it’s easy to fall for the “cover” from every angle.

Having got through 15% of the text, I did what my professional deformation dictates and began fantasising about a screen adaptation — who would be best to play whom, from among Western actors, naturally.

It was some 5 minutes into our search for the best actor for the lead that the AI and I stumbled on the news that Matty Manson is the pen name of a Russian writer and that her text — for all the rough edges, which I had been putting down precisely to translation — was Russian in the original.

Pros: I now know about an actor who’d be perfect for the role of Vinny, name of Louis Partridge. Cons: I feel cheated as hell.

In short, don’t repeat my mistakes: check where a text comes from before you put together your dream cast.

item.title: Tony: A Sweet Film with Gastronomic Charm
item.description: Tony is a sweet, inessential film that is best not watched on an empty stomach.
item.content:encoded:
Tony is a sweet, inessential film that is best not watched on an empty stomach.

The origin story of the famous chef Anthony Bourdain, played by the darkly charismatic Dominic Sessa, is full of twists that look hackneyed at first glance: the cocksure young man doesn’t get his scholarship, the girl he loves turns out to have another boyfriend, and in a provincial town Tony has his wallet cleaned out on the very first night (a wallet stuffed, by the way, with money stolen from his parents’ house). Life (wearing the face of Antonio Banderas) diligently (though not to the point of collapse) douses Tony with ice-cold water so that the young man might amount to something, and to some degree this even works as the engine of the plot.

What hooked me, though, was the rapid transformation promised in the trailer: I decided to watch the film to find out how someone who saw himself as a writer turned, over a 3-month break, into a cook by vocation.

For all the scope the subject offers for passions to unfold on screen, the film is surprisingly sterile: the only emotionally engaging scene is one spectacular kitchen rush. And it seems (given how predictable a biopic is) there was never much call to worry about the fate of Tony himself. The place of the hero you want to root for is taken by his colleague and pal Sal (Leo Woodall), an easy-going, open-hearted guy who collects vices and splinters from the door frames of the bedrooms he has managed to get into. Next to a supporting character like that, with a far more dramatic fate, Tony himself comes off second best.

But the best thing the film demonstrates, both in words and by its own example, is that it may be better to become at least someone than to remain no one.

item.title: Connor Storrie, Saint Laurent and a Pop-Culture Phenomenon
item.description: I love it when someone explores fascinating (to me) pop-culture phenomena. It’s about the Connor Storrie phenomenon in the Saint Laurent ad campaign.
item.content:encoded:
I love it when someone explores fascinating (to me) pop-culture phenomena, and I’ve just lost myself in a long-read post by a colleague.

It’s about the Connor Storrie phenomenon in the Saint Laurent ad campaign. And I think you can mentally add Hudson Williams, his co-star in the series about hockey players, who did a shoot for Balenciaga. We saw them in the respective outfits, by the way, back around the Oscars.

All the same, film and the power of fan communities are a great thing, and at times they affect the world veeery tangibly. Even these fashion houses show how, between the 1990s and today, the policy of “the face of the brand will be models” has given way to “the face of the brand will be people who bring a trail of cultural associations and a certain ideology with them”. And what other public figures can be as rich in context as actors?

Especially sobering is the answer to the question “Why would a high-fashion brand want the hero of teenage dreams and the cause of girlish tears, when his audience doesn’t even have much money to spend?” I kept wondering about it, and now, having read the post, I’ve realised there’s a whole strategy behind it.

item.title: Coyote vs. Acme: A Winning Mix of Animation and Corporate Critique
item.description: Coyote vs. Acme turns out to be a mix of unexpected ingredients that works as well as it possibly could: animation and live action, cultural clichés about Albuquerque and a critique of corporations.
item.content:encoded:
Coyote vs. Acme turns out to be a mix of unexpected ingredients that works as well as it possibly could: animation and live action, cultural clichés about Albuquerque (thank you, Vince Gilligan) and a critique of corporations.

The story of a cartoon character who sets out to fight for justice (and for his tasty dinner) with the help of a human lawyer is far more interesting on screen than it sounds on paper. The film is an absolute sweetheart: for practically all ages, with humour that is not simple-minded yet not bloodthirsty either, and with some wonderfully spot-on casting (this is the funniest John Cena I have ever seen). And also with a touching story of enmity that turns out to have been hiding a friendship all along (I am not warped in the slightest).

Because it’s set in Albuquerque and the lawyer hero is very fond of outrageous advertising, I kept wanting to picture Bob Odenkirk’s Saul Goodman in his place :) But even without that, Coyote vs. Acme is captivating: behind its apparent simplicity the film hides a great deal of charm. In Russian cinemas from tomorrow — I strongly recommend going and having a great time.

item.title: The 2x2 Idents by the Artists of Prostye Veshchi
item.description: The TV channel 2x2 has teamed up with artists with mental disabilities from the design bureau Prostye Veshchi to create television idents.
item.content:encoded:
An off-topic post about a very humane initiative

The TV channel 2x2 (Russia’s animation channel) has teamed up with artists with mental disabilities from the design bureau Prostye Veshchi (“Simple Things”, an inclusive workshop in St Petersburg) to create television idents: five artists came up with the characters and stories, and 2x2 digitised them and made animated idents, which have been airing on the channel since 1 September.

The result is bright and unique — and it’s cool that things like this are making their way onto the telly at a time when it’s getting harder and harder to find anything interesting. And drawings like these, by the way, can not only be seen on screen but also bought as souvenirs from the Prostye Veshchi shop: I personally got glued to the page with the notebooks and postcards.

item.title: CTRL+FEST 2.0 Asks “What Next?”: Films That Look for the Answer
item.description: The CTRL+FEST 2.0 festival is asking “What next?”, and, as in any baffling situation, I decided to think about which films might help find the answer.
item.content:encoded:
The CTRL+FEST 2.0 festival is asking “What next?”, and, as in any baffling situation, I decided to think about which films might help find the answer. Plenty of films from recent years fit the bill; they are all different and sometimes contradict one another, but it is in argument that truth is born, so I think that’s for the best. The conflict you can spell out for each of these films also holds an answer to the question “What next?”

  • Everything Everywhere All at Once (2021): when every branch of reality is laid out in plain view, yet it’s so hard to choose the one that is yours

  • Rag Union («Тряпичный союз», Tryapichny soyuz, 2014): when the future is made of pushing one thing and watching another fall

  • In Limbo («Межсезонье», 2021): when the search for the right answer turns into a tragedy

item.title: Hard to Be a God: No Bombast in Episode One, and a Finale Worth Sticking Around For
item.description: The first episode of Hard to Be a God has an absolutely wonderful aura: none of the knock-you-flat bombast that is traditional for Russian fantasy.
item.content:encoded:
2 September 2026

The first episode of Hard to Be a God (Trudno byt bogom) has an absolutely wonderful aura: none of the knock-you-flat bombast that is traditional for Russian fantasy.

This take on the Strugatskys makes no claim to be the fundamental last word; on the contrary, you can tell it was made by contemporaries for a contemporary audience. Sergey Bezrukov’s Don Condor lets slip, every now and then, the smirk of Belov from Brigada. Nikita Kologrivy also does what he does well: in the very first episode he is already mouthing off at the local king in the raised tones of Koshchey from The Boy’s Word.

And so, in the small details and shades of intonation, every actor is, to my mind, 100% in the right place: Viktoria Isakova, Irina Pautova, Lev Zulkarnaev, Ravshana Kurkova, Alexander Demidov and many, many more. The audience chuckled approvingly when the screenwriter Andrey Zolotarev, playing the treasurer, nodded with great dignity in a brief scene in the first episode. I wonder whether his character will get a big story arc? :)

A particular pleasure was Aleksandar Radojičić as Don Rumata, the protagonist through whose eyes we first get to know the world of Arkanar. Unlike the actors listed above, he carries no fixed associations for the mass audience, and that is great, because it means we cannot predict his character — real intrigue. Also, in real life Aleksandar has the sweetest Serbian accent, and the one thing I could not work out while watching was whether he has been dubbed completely or left with a slight accent, as a sign that the hero, even by local standards, has come from somewhere very, very far away. To my mind, it would be great to use the actor’s natural accent to convey the hero’s otherness.

Also, colleagues at Wink (the Russian streaming service) have made a very informative (and entertaining) long read on the universe of Hard to Be a God: you can take a quiz to find out which Observer you are and leaf through dossiers on the characters. Alongside the series (which, as you will have gathered, I plan to keep watching), I will be reading the Strugatskys’ novel and watching Aleksei German’s feature-film version: I want to immerse myself completely in this metaverse.

18 October 2026

Getting to the finale of Hard to Be a God turned out to be harder than I expected, but it was all worth it.

First, the difficulties: to my mind, from about the midpoint the series starts to feel cramped inside its own cluttered world. The rhythm falters, some episodes are far more densely packed than others, and so the viewer’s engagement suffers too (mine did, at any rate).

On the other hand, Aleksandar Radojičić’s Don Rumata was a joy. He is detached enough for an Observer and yet sincerely interested in experiencing what mortals experience. That is both what saves him and what lets him down; here everything depends on how you feel about the finale. In my view, it never hurts to remember the price at which the passage from dark times to light is won.

item.title: Chudo: A Graphic Novel About an Angel in Yekaterinburg
item.description: It’s a short graphic novel (or comic, whichever you prefer) about the adventures of an angel who has come down from heaven to Yekaterinburg.
item.content:encoded:
If you want to lift your mood, look at the world with renewed love and give your soul a rest, you will need Chudo («Чудо», “Miracle”).

It’s a short graphic novel (or comic, whichever you prefer) about the adventures of an angel who has come down from heaven to Yekaterinburg. He longs to see the human world, and for guides he gets the feisty Masha and her starry-eyed younger brother Tima. But what matters most in this comic is the small pieces that add up to an utterly inimitable whole:

  • A unique style unlike anything else: the golden glow of the angel’s wings, the lights of the city at night and the twinkling windows of tower blocks burst through the screen (or the page). If “dopamine” is a word that can be applied to comics, it applies to Chudo.

  • A fresh take on the well-established plot of a heavenly being visiting Earth. We’ve seen it in the film Moy paren — angel (“My Boyfriend Is an Angel”), in the series Good Omens and in plenty of other places. But transposed to a contemporary Russian metropolis, with moments from young people’s lives, the news on TV, and jokes about working in food service and about a father who has left the family, it feels absolutely superb.

  • An infectious kindness in everything that happens, which never slides into cloying moralising about Christian values. I don’t know how the author achieved this effect, but the plot asks for no buy-in whatsoever when it comes to faith or other sensitive matters: what takes shape before us is simply the story of one introduction to Earth, and the verdict of a hero who has seen humanity in all its guises.

And yes, I’ve already added Chudo to my list of dream screen adaptations.

item.title: Big Pharma: The Pleasure of Its Visual Language
item.description: I’ve started Big Pharma, and this show’s visual language is giving me real, genuine pleasure. In short, you can’t take your eyes off it.
item.content:encoded:
I’ve started Big Pharma, and this show’s visual language is giving me real, genuine pleasure.

Cinematographer Batyr Morgachev uses a fisheye lens here, and wide-angle perspective, and swirly bokeh (that blurred background around Goroshko that seems to curl as things move). In short, you can’t take your eyes off it.

All this, plus the cast’s pinpoint performances, makes up for the slight sense of contrivance I get from how lavishly the main characters live: by all appearances a no-name researcher who has spent a couple of decades working on a single drug, and his plastic-surgeon son, whose wealth you can believe in, of course, but not to that extent. Even so, I’ll definitely keep watching: this is an extremely gripping pharmaceutical thriller.

item.title: Organized Criminal Group: Yuri Chursin as Conscience
item.description: I’ve started watching the series OPG, intrigued by Yuri Chursin in the role of the protagonist’s Conscience — the protagonist, in turn, is played by Pyotr Buslov.
item.content:encoded:
I’ve started watching the series OPG («ОПГ», “Organized Criminal Group”), intrigued by Yuri Chursin in the role of the protagonist’s Conscience — the protagonist, in turn, is played by Pyotr Buslov.

His character, nicknamed Vorkuta, gets out of prison after something like 20 years inside, with a clingy Conscience trailing along behind him. As a result, a bodiless entity with Yuri Chursin’s face makes the former racketeer apologise to all his victims from the 1990s. The premise is interesting, but I have a couple of observations about the details:

1️⃣ First, I can’t shake the thought that this looks an awful lot like the central idea of Yura Borisov’s character in the film Captain Volkonogov Escaped. There, he wanted to apologise to the surviving relatives of victims of the repressions. It will be interesting to see how a similar motivation plays out in comic circumstances and with a 1990s theme.

2️⃣ Second, the filming location really bothers me: for the cityscapes of the fictional small town of Dalnemorsk, where OPG is set, they for some reason picked a highly recognisable square in Moscow’s Kitay-Gorod, with a view of buildings in an unmistakably Moscow style, one you hardly associate with provincial seaside towns. Unfortunately, that somehow undermines, right away, your ability to trust what is happening on screen.

On the plus side, I’m genuinely delighted by Chursin’s transformations: as Conscience (that is, an entity invisible to everyone but his “owner”) he is constantly changing guises, and does it inventively every time. By the second episode I already wanted a spin-off with Conscience, as he plays it, in the lead. It distantly recalls (today is my day for spotting overlaps) Evgeny Tkachuk’s work in the recent The Dog of Many Tomorrows (Kosmicheskaya sobaka Lida, “Lida the Space Dog”), where this was also done with great inventiveness and on a truly grand scale.

item.title: What the New Spider-Man and The Odyssey Have in Common
item.description: It’s striking how these two summer blockbusters actually echo each other. The existential crisis has officially become a plot for mainstream cinema.
item.content:encoded:
What do the new Spider-Man and The Odyssey have in common?

It’s striking how these two summer blockbusters actually echo each other. In The Odyssey the hero has forgotten himself and, roughly speaking, where he was going. In Spider-Man it’s the other way round: everyone around the hero has forgotten him, and because of that he no longer knows where to turn. By and large, these are two dimensions of one and the same phenomenon; the only difference is whether the personal crisis we see on screen is expressed outwardly or inwardly.

And Tom Holland (not only he, as you can see from the meme, but that’s beside the point right now) has got to stand, through his characters, both on the outside of the protagonist’s suffering (Odysseus’s son Telemachus, who is trying to cope with the world somehow while his father remembers where he belongs) and on the inside (Peter Parker himself). The actor really did land two roles from the “choose your type of existential crisis” series — and both, happily, come across as convincing and rounded, as portrayals by a contemporary, for contemporaries.

So it turns out that the biggest blockbusters of 2026 centre on heroes who are not so much fighting evil as trying to redefine themselves, recover a sense of belonging and work out where to go next. The existential crisis has officially become a plot for mainstream cinema — apparently because it has stopped being something purely personal.

item.title: Olivia Wilde’s The Invite: Go In Without Expectations, and Keep an Eye on the Costumes
item.description: This dramedy, staged like a chamber play, has plenty of surprises in store. The film deserves separate credit for the pair of neighbours played by Penélope Cruz and Edward Norton.
item.content:encoded:
16 August 2026

The film The Invite is best watched without any firmly formed expectations.

This dramedy, staged like a chamber play, has plenty of surprises in store. Joe and Angela, a long-married couple whose relationship has been knocked about by life, played by Seth Rogen and Olivia Wilde (who is also the film’s director), have long since stopped talking to each other in any way other than quarrelling. Joe, a music teacher, is unhappy with his job, his pupils and his everyday life, while Angela, a housewife, is looking for new acquaintances and suddenly invites round the neighbours, who frankly drive him up the wall because they are noisy at night 🔞

It sounds like the standard set-up for a comedy about a couple putting their relationship back together after one decisive encounter, but in fact The Invite is nothing of the kind. Practically a television play for four characters, it comes with a stunningly well-judged backdrop of classical music, and is full of shifts in emotional register and play with the visual side of things.

The film deserves separate credit for the pair of neighbours played by Penélope Cruz and Edward Norton. As a duo they have stunning chemistry, but each on their own has a simply magnetic energy too. I especially like how Cruz’s character, next to Norton, comes across as a kind of Tyler Durden: she instantly sees through the psychology of whoever she is talking to and manipulates them masterfully. One of the best female characters I’ve seen lately, and one of the coolest ensemble casts all round.

17 August 2026

By the way, pay special attention to how the characters of The Invite are dressed.

The hosts, Joe and Angela, wear clothes in dull pastel shades (washed-out mint and faded denim), which each go with the flat’s interior but don’t harmonise with each other at all. And indeed, the two of them have long been a poor match, tormented by the boredom of their life.

We see a quite different combination with the guests: Pina and Hawk are dressed to go with each other. Both wear black tops, which underline their deep bond and at the same time their air of mystery (and they did, it has to be said, turn up on distinctly mysterious vibes).

The costume designer Arianne Phillips said that she deliberately made Joe’s and Angela’s costumes clash in shade — it is an important marker of their relationship. The black on the guest couple she explained as a symbol of togetherness and mutual chemistry. And the simple silhouettes were chosen to keep viewers from drawing premature conclusions about the characters.

item.title: Daneliya’s Heads and Tails: If Brother Were a Rom-Com
item.description: If Brother had been a rom-com with a happy ending, you would have got Heads and Tails. It’s a great piece of luck that Georgiy Daneliya actually made it, in 1995.
item.content:encoded:
If Brother had been a rom-com with a happy ending, you would have got Heads and Tails. It’s a great piece of luck that Georgiy Daneliya actually made it, in 1995.

The plot is simple enough: Oleg Chagin (Kirill Pirogov, who, incidentally, found fame in Brother 2) comes back to Moscow from a work stint in the far north to win his beloved back from the husband she has suddenly acquired. In Moscow, naturally, nobody is waiting for our hero — nothing but a fateful meeting with Zina Prishchepkina, an ordinary canteen worker played by a veeery young Polina Kutepova. What follows are adventures of the “just a normal Tuesday in Russia” kind: the hero accidentally saves the life of a woman he doesn’t know, meets a New Russian (an unrecognisable Leonid Yarmolnik), instantly becomes his friend, and then falls victim to Gypsies, capitalism and hasty conclusions.

The most precious thing in the film is the inimitable aura of an era — the turn of the millennium — that is amply represented on film, yet here it isn’t plastered with the usual clichés but shot as if through the eyes of a witness watching what becomes of an ordinary contemporary. The views of 1990s Moscow are mesmerising too: the Oktyabr cinema alone flashes past a dozen or so times, as if to remind us that in thirty years everything in the city has changed — and nothing.

But the main thing is Chagin as played by Kirill Pirogov: a real hidden treasure in the line of generation-defining heroes like Kostik in The Pokrovsky Gate, Bananan in Assa, Ivan in Messenger Boy and Danila in Brother. Chagin is lost, cynical and crafty in moderation, but not in the least cruel or underhand, and he hasn’t lost his humanity. He is, of course, a protagonist with a full set of negative qualities, but, as if on purpose, he switches them on only with the best of intentions.

item.title: Obsession: The Year’s Most Talked-About Horror Turns Out to Be a Comedy Too
item.description: During the first half of Obsession I laughed practically every five minutes. Director Curry Barker creates terror with a minimal set of tools.
item.content:encoded:
I would never have thought that the most talked-about horror film of 2026 would also turn out to be an excellent comedy.

During the first half of Obsession I laughed practically every five minutes. The awkwardness of Bear’s attempts at socialising is exaggerated to such a degree that it comes across as an out-and-out comic device.

But once the horror side of it gets going, the impression it leaves is, of course, indelible. Director Curry Barker creates terror with a minimal set of tools — what triggers you most is the characters’ unnatural, instantaneous swings of emotion. Inde Navarrette in particular does something blood-curdling with nothing but her facial expressions. Even when you notice, here and there, a dummy with some CGI in place of a human figure (the film has a modest budget), it is still outweighed by the shock you’ve already been through.

The concept itself — the body being taken away from the mind (as in Get Out) — leaves you frozen. And the theme, of course, is a burning one — both that love is blind and that you can’t make someone love you. An unequivocal recommendation to watch (though maybe not over dinner).
